meta.title: Getting started with Claude for software development
meta.author: adsouza

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
One thing I'd note is that the gap between https://claude.ai and Claude Code has been quietly closing over the past few months - in an undocumented and little-discussed way.

Regular Claude has access to a Linux container which it can edit files in, execute code in, and do the coding agent thing of writing code, executing that code and then fixing any errors and iterating towards a solution that works.

It can also perform limited read-only network operations in that container - most notably it can install additional packages from PyPI and NPM and can clone public repos from GitHub.

That's limited compared to Claude Code which can be run on almost any machine with no restrictions, but for a lot of coding work the regular Claude restrictions let you get a very long way.

I frequently prototype new features for my various open source projects using normal Claude chat - start by telling it to clone my public repo from GitHub, then have it read the code and brainstorm with me, then have it start building prototypes of new ideas.

Claude.ai also has artifacts, a wonderful feature where it can build full HTML+JS single page apps directly inside the Claude interface. These are restricted in what they can talk to (no fetching JSON data from external APIs for example) but can still load NPM libraries from a CDN and can even make API calls back to Anthropic (a feature called Claudeception) and store and retrieve simple key/value data from a server-side store.

So there's actually a whole lot of fun coding stuff you can try with Claude alone.

comments.author: jonathannen
comments.text:
In my current AI workflow I try to maximize use of claude.ai for many of the reasons you mention.

Plus the container part is free (somehow?), which is extraordinary. And as you say, you can really do quite a bit. I'm currently working on having it generate screenshots w/ playwright of changes it's made.

comments.author: strugee
comments.text:
What draws you to Claude web over Claude Code? (Or to put the question another way, even if Claude web is getting better, why use it if Claude Code is still strictly "more capable"?)

Not having to worry about sandboxing the Claude Code agent would be top of my personal list, but I'm curious what your reasons are since I'm still a beginner at these tools.

comments.author: jonathannen
comments.text:
If you're starting out, I'd definitely recommend Claude Code in the terminal -- or whatever IDE. vscode Claude is pretty capable if you happen to be in that tool.

Claude locally has a quite limited permission set when starting out - as you grow you can add skills/scripts/cli you can layer in what you need. A lot of people open up "dangerously use permissions" or give claude access to the kitchen sink, but in my experience that's not necessary. Especially if once you start on your own skills (but that's another day if you're starting out).

The primary reason I use claude.ai is to help me max-out developing in parallel (I try to have 20+ tasks ongoing at a time). On the occasion I'm hacking back and forth on something I'll use the terminal.

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text: claude web is strictly safer. no localhost access etc

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
Yeah, it's pretty hard to shoot yourself in the foot with https://claude.ai - beyond falling victim to LLM psychosis.

I've been trying to encourage people who want to experiment with vibe coding to start with Claude artifacts precisely because it's hard to hurt your own machine or leak other people's data with them.

comments.author: adsouza
comments.text: Another thing the web app seems to have over at least the VS Code plugin for Claude Code is that it is able to scour the web for answers.

comments.author: simonw
comments.text: Claude Code in the terminal can run web searches, I haven't spent time with the VS Code plugin.

comments.author: strugee
comments.text:
At first, this article convinced me to not invest more time in LLMs... because I'm currently in the beginning stages of learning Vim! (After ~a decade of being a beginner to intermediate Emacs user.)

But... I actually progressed naturally in much the same way this article is suggesting you progress. I started with Claude web and dropped down to Claude Code really just because it was convenient to have it operate on multiple files. So I've bookmarked and may revisit the followups at some point.
